cards.back: An integral defined using a limit because of an infinite interval or an unbounded integrand.
An accumulated exposure measure given by integrating concentration over time.
A series Σ1/nᵖ; it converges exactly when p>1.
A bound or expression for the error left after truncating a Taylor expansion.
Accumulated mechanical energy transfer W=∫F·dx along a displacement.
The integral of a function over an interval divided by interval length.
Distance from a power-series center within which the series converges; endpoints need separate tests.
The error between a function and its finite Taylor polynomial, bounded using higher derivatives.
Total = ∫ rate dt; units: (amount/time) × time.
T = h[q₀/2 + … + qₙ/2]; S = (h/3)[q₀ + 4q₁ + 2q₂ + … + qₙ] with n even.
|E| ≤ (b − a)h²/12 · max|f″|; convex functions are overestimated; halving h quarters the bound.
∫₀^∞ e^(−kt) dt = 1/k converges; ∫₁^∞ dt/t diverges; ∫₁^∞ dt/t² converges.
Pₙ(x) = Σ f⁽ᵏ⁾(a)(x − a)ᵏ/k! for k ≤ n.
|Rₙ| ≤ M|x − a|ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)! with M bounding |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾| on the interval.
1 − e^(−kt) ≈ kt with relative error about kt/2.
ln(1 + x) ≈ x and sin θ ≈ θ (radians) only for small arguments.
Substitution reverses the chain rule; parts reverses the product rule; partial fractions separates a rational integrand after division if needed.
Transform both endpoint bounds or return to the original variable before evaluating. Keep domains and units consistent.
Differentiate a candidate primitive and compare it with the original integrand; check poles separately.
ln|x| has derivative 1/x on each nonzero interval; it does not justify endpoint cancellation across zero.
Integrate on a finite nonsingular interval and take the required endpoint limit. Every improper part must converge separately.
∫₁∞x⁻ᵖ converges for p>1; ∫₀¹x⁻ᵖ converges for p<1.
A convergent nonnegative upper bound guarantees convergence below it; a divergent lower bound guarantees divergence above it.
Symmetric cancellation is a separate definition. It does not replace convergence of each ordinary improper part.
aₙ→0 is necessary for Σaₙ to converge but not sufficient; inspect partial sums or use a justified test.
A limiting absolute ratio below 1 gives absolute convergence; above 1 gives divergence; equal to 1 is inconclusive.
For indices 0 through N and |r|<1, the exact tail is r^(N+1)/(1−r). Count indices explicitly.
For positive decreasing f with a convergent tail, ∫_(N+1)∞f≤Σ_(n=N+1)∞f(n)≤∫_N∞f.
Absolute convergence means Σ|aₙ| converges. Conditional convergence means the signed series converges while the magnitudes do not.
For nonnegative decreasing magnitudes tending to zero, the error after N terms is at most the first omitted magnitude.
Under those conditions, the exact sum lies between consecutive partial sums; the remainder has the first omitted sign.
A bound that fails a tolerance is inconclusive about actual error. A successful bound is deterministic, not a confidence interval.
The radius defines interior absolute convergence. Test each real endpoint separately to determine brackets.
Power series can be integrated and differentiated inside their radius; endpoints can change convergence behavior.
Track x−c, normalized arguments and the first term when shifting indices or substituting variables.
A function may be defined outside an expansion radius; its finite polynomial is evaluable there but need not approximate it.
The coefficient of (x−a)ʲ is f^(j)(a)/j!. Degree and number of nonzero terms are distinct.
Bound the next derivative over the entire interval connecting center and evaluation point, then multiply by distance power divided by factorial.
A pointwise bound B(x) yields accumulated error at most ∫B; output units include the interval units.
Separate truncation, rounding, uncertain inputs and model discrepancy. A Taylor remainder controls only the stated mathematical truncation.
Area uses strip or sector area; volume uses cross-sectional area or shells; arc length uses √((x′)²+(y′)²)dt.
A radial cross-sectional integral needs 2πr dr. Dividing by πR² gives an area average.
Parametric length counts the traced distance over the specified bounds, including repeated traversals.
Cross-sectional integration of a volumetric concentration gives amount per length; a cylinder length is required for total amount.
Integrate force over displacement; composite rules need the correct spacing and weights. N·m is J.
On a valid interval, bound the exact remaining integrand and integrate that bound. Positive omitted terms give an underestimate.
A constant force offset contributes offset times displacement to work. Averaging balanced repeats does not remove it.
Agreement with a known synthetic generating formula checks the calculation, not whether a real device follows that model.
The quotient must be 0/0 or ∞/∞, the functions must satisfy local differentiability and denominator conditions, and the derivative quotient must have a limit.
After each derivative step, reclassify the new quotient; stop when the limit is directly available.
Rewrite a product, difference or positive-base power as an equivalent quotient before considering L’Hôpital’s rule.
Check dominant terms or simplify when possible; L’Hôpital’s rule is a theorem for eligible quotients, not a general differentiation shortcut.
With an odd power, save one factor and convert the rest with sin² + cos² = 1; with both powers even, halve the angle: sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2, cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2.
∫ tan x dx = −ln|cos x| + C and ∫ sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C, valid only on intervals where cos x ≠ 0.
√(a² − x²): x = a sin θ; √(a² + x²): x = a tan θ; √(x² − a²): x = a sec θ. Choose θ ranges that keep the substitution one-to-one and the root non-negative, then convert the bounds.
Rewrite a quadratic as (x − h)² ± k² to reach an arctangent, arcsine or substitution form; factor out a leading coefficient first and check where the quadratic is positive.
For a decaying integrand, the omitted tail ∫_T^∞ shrinks as T grows, so a tolerance gives a smallest sufficient cutoff, found by solving tail(T) ≤ tolerance.
If |Rₙ(x)| ≤ M xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)! on [0, b], the integrated error is at most M bⁿ⁺²/(n + 2)!.
A small remainder certifies closeness to the stipulated function; it says nothing about whether that function describes any external system.

cards.front: Which small element produces surface area about the x-axis?
cards.back: A nonnegative radius times circumference factor two pi and the generating arc length; disk-volume and radial-annulus elements answer different questions.

cards.front: What must be stated before integrating a geometric boundary?
cards.back: The requested quantity, generating axis, interval/coverage and inclusion of end caps; an outline alone does not identify the correct element.

cards.front: Can a once-traced curve generate a multiply covered surface?
cards.back: Yes. Rotation can map different generating-curve portions to the same surface. Check the surface map, not just the planar traversal.

cards.front: Why can a numerically accurate integral still give the wrong geometric quantity?
cards.back: The integrator evaluates the supplied element and bounds; it cannot decide whether they describe volume, lateral area, end caps or repeated coverage.

cards.front: How do pointwise and uniform claims differ?
cards.back: Pointwise convergence permits an index depending on the evaluation point; a uniform bound controls all points with one index on the stated interval.

cards.front: Why can a fixed sample grid mislead for a narrowing sequence?
cards.back: It can miss a moving or shrinking concentration of area even when every sampled value is small; pointwise observations do not control an integral.

cards.front: What extra claim is needed beyond smoothness for an infinite Taylor representation?
cards.back: One must justify that the remainder tends to zero on the claimed domain. Finite differentiability/remainder statements alone do not supply that limit.

cards.front: Why do different termwise operations need separate hypotheses?
cards.back: A bound sufficient for the original series or its integral need not control derivatives, whose terms and endpoint behavior can differ.

cards.front: What does a mixed-method report need beyond two decimal answers?
cards.back: Structure-based choices, complete transformations, antiderivative residuals/domains, boundary terms and an independent numerical comparison.

cards.front: Why keep one shared cutoff for this partial-fraction limit?
cards.back: The original convergent integrand can be integrated before the limit; subtracting two separately divergent integrals as infinity minus infinity is invalid.

cards.front: What distinguishes volume, lateral area and capped area?
cards.back: Their small elements, dimensions and boundary pieces differ. State the requested object before choosing an integral.

cards.front: Why distinguish a weighted quantile from an average?
cards.back: The half-amount radius solves a cumulative integral with a declared domain; it is neither half the radius nor the area-average density.

cards.front: How does a slow tail challenge numerical convergence claims?
cards.back: Finite partial sums can look stable while a positive infinite tail still diverges or remains large. Use the theorem hypotheses and a bound with a clear index convention.

cards.front: Which labels prevent off-by-one and endpoint mistakes?
cards.back: State first included index, last included index or term count, first omitted term, series center/radius and separately tested boundary points.

cards.front: Why does this approximation field require six significant figures?
cards.back: Three figures round estimate and reference to the same value. Preserve sufficient display precision and keep truncation, reference error and display rounding separate.

cards.front: Why distinguish polynomial degree, term count and a sufficient bound?
cards.back: Zero/parity structure and index conventions change the count, while a conservative guarantee is not automatically an exact error or a necessary condition.

f̄ = (1/(b − a))∫ₐᵇ f dx: total divided by length. It lies between the least and greatest values of f, and a continuous f attains it at some c (mean value theorem for integrals). An average rate is total over time.
A density totals by slicing: M = ∫ λ dx, or cells N = ∫ n dx. The weighted average position is x̄ = ∫ x w dx / ∫ w dx, between the endpoints and toward the denser end.

f ≥ 0 and ∫ f = 1. P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f; a single value has probability 0; f may exceed 1. Mean μ = ∫ x f dx; the median m solves ∫ f from the lower end to m = 1/2. Exponential: f = λe^(−λt), P(T > t) = e^(−λt), mean 1/λ, median ln 2/λ.

A tail integral runs to infinity. A density can have total 1 and an infinite mean: f = 1/x² on x ≥ 1 gives ∫ dx/x, the p = 1 case. The bell curve has no elementary antiderivative, so probabilities use numerical integration.
